AI and Mathematics

What is the role of mathematics in the age of AI?

Terrance tao’s 2026 ICM address invited listeners to consider a thought experiment - if AI has unbounded ability to solve problems, what should it’s role be? Just a few weeks later, OpenAI announced a solution to the Navier-Stokes Millenium prize problem. The world is now asking what is the role of humans in Mathematics when computers can solve and validate (via automated proof checkers like LEAN) potentially every well-posed problem.

In our moment in time there are many factors which obscure the philosophical question underlying the variety of answers to the titular question. “Lucky for us, history is cyclic and the mathematical community has been in a similar situation before. The 4 color problem was the most famous example of a computer assisted proof before the age of AI. Kenneth Appel and Wolfgang Haken proved, by checking 1936 cases using a computer, that all maps can be colored with 4 distinct colors such that no neighbouring countries had the same color. It is an irrefutable fact that their method was sufficient for establishing that this theorem is true but their proof was met with criticism. Apart from map printers who really didn’t want to buy a fifth shade of ink, did the verification of this fact do good for mathematics and for humanity?

Thurston famously wrote We are not trying to meet some abstract production quota of definitions, theorems and proofs. The measure of our [mathematician’s] success is whether what we do enables people to understand and think more clearly and effectively about math. Applying this viewpoint I claim that knowledge of the “verification” of these 1936 cases don’t meaningfully help us to understand the structure of graph colorings. In the best case senario, studying these cases further, with the knowledge that all of them can be 4 coloured, might give new insights. However, the problem being “solved” leaves no glory/credit for other mathematicians. A second proof - even if it’s not computer generated - doesn’t count for as much which might prevent a more insightful solution. I believe that disagreements on the value of machine generated proofs fundamental comes down to disagreements about what mathematics is?

One view of mathematics is that it is akin to exploration: in the abstract space of ideas, there exist pairs of axioms and conclusions and mathematics seeks to determine which pairs are true and false. In this analogy mathematicians group ideas into geographical features (subselds of math) and draw up maps (publishing textbooks and papers) to discover more facts. I think this view of maths is very easy to motivate - it’s the search for the truth - which is why mathematicians present this view to the public and it’s “platonic” devotion to rigour gives mathematics prestige. However this idealised version of mathematics is anti-human. Memorizing facts isn’t what humans are designed for. We build computers and databases (Mathlib and LEAN) to contain all that data so that we can think about these facts. A more human view of mathematics is precisely this. It’s fun to think logically about problems and mathematics is the structure humans have built (our notation, our journals, our community) to enable current and future mathematicians to keep having fun.

Now I want to stress that I don’t believe mathematics is a frivolous pursuit. In the process of solving fun and interesting problems, mathematicians have, accidentally, built something that is unreasonably effective at solving problems in the real world. We invented linear algebra to solve polynomial equations and our efforts to standardise and disseminate these techniques played a role in almost all modern technology. We haven’t made the clear to the public because it’s a lot easier to convince governments and universities to fund a rigorous factual exploration than a group of people who like fun brainteasers.

To complete this argument, we still need to demonstrate that these byproducts of mathematical research will continue to be useful. To address the discourse around AI directly, I think a lot of people heralding the end of mathematics have the tacit assumption that AI will soon be able to optimally run society. Putting aside the dystopian questions that raises about autonomy, the biggest obstruction is the AI alignment problem - how do we ensure that any AI system is aligned with the goals of humanity. This is a highly non-trivial problem with potentially species ending consequence is we get it wrong. I might be biased but I believe that, for this and many other problems that our species is facing, curiosity driven mathematics is our best shot.
